strengths: Novel and important problem: First systematic study of sycophancy in Video-LLMs, extending prior text-only work to multimodal domain with temporal complexity
Well-designed benchmark: ViSE provides 367 carefully curated videos with 6,367 questions, comprehensive two-stage filtering, 7 sycophancy types, and diverse question/prompt scenarios
Rigorous empirical analysis: Evaluates 9 Video-LLM variants, reveals systematic patterns of vulnerability across model sizes/families, and provides detailed cross-model comparisons
Practical mitigation strategies: Both key-frame selection and representation steering show effectiveness; ablation studies (Table 7) validate approach over baselines
Comprehensive experimental coverage: Detailed investigation of how sycophancy varies by model scale, question type, and prompt structure with clear metric definitions
Transparency and reproducibility: Extensive appendices with prompts, experimental settings, mathematical formulations, and computational resource specifications
Clear presentation: Well-structured writing with effective figures illustrating the problem and comprehensive examples across multiple domains
weaknesses: Limited generalizability of mitigation strategies: Key-frame selection fails on LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering requires model-specific vector computation and per-model hyperparameter tuning (α), undermining 'training-free' claim
Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars, or variance estimates; single runs reported without replication; CRS results noted as limited by small sample size
Relatively small benchmark scale: 367 videos is modest; 87.8% video overlap between filtering stages raises data leakage concerns; limited to short factual clips from three datasets

Limited theoretical insight: Paper is primarily empirical; lacks mechanistic explanation for why video-based sycophancy occurs; minimal investigation of visual features/temporal patterns triggering behavior; doesn't distinguish language vs. multimodal-fusion sources

Modest improvements in some scenarios: Key-frame selection improvements vary (4.77 for 'Explicitly Endorse X'); representation steering results degrade dramatically with σ≥0.75; no comparison with alternative mitigation approaches

Representation steering method limitations: Only tested on 3 models; requires identifying optimal layer per model; hyperparameter α tuning contradicts 'training-free' framing; lacks theoretical justification; no evaluation of side effects on other capabilities

Benchmark design limitations: Two-stage filtering creates specific hard cases not necessarily representative; question types show extreme MSS variance (22.54 vs 9.55); 'visual grounding as solution' doesn't apply uniformly to all sycophancy types

Insufficient evaluation of scope and applicability: No user studies validating real-world impact; temporal dynamics (claimed as key differentiator) underexplored; only covers existing models at publication time; unclear transferability to new architectures

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem of sycophancy in Video-LLMs, with clear relevance to multimodal model reliability
Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark (ViSE) featuring 367 carefully curated videos, 6,367 annotated questions across 7 sycophancy types and multiple reasoning categories
Thorough empirical analysis systematically investigating how model size, question complexity, and prompt intensity affect sycophancy across 9 model variants
Two practical training-free mitigation strategies with clear evidence of effectiveness: key-frame selection (MSS reduction up to -22) and representation steering (MSS reduction up to -27)
Rigorous methodology including well-defined metrics (MSS, CRS), thoughtful ablation studies, and detailed experimental documentation supporting reproducibility
Excellent presentation with clear figures, comprehensive tables, well-organized appendices, and illustrative case studies that effectively communicate findings
Acknowledges limitations transparently, including scope of models tested and generalization concerns for proposed methods
weaknesses: Limited generalization of mitigation strategies: key-frame selection fails for LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering requires model-specific calibration, limiting applicability to new architectures

Relatively narrow model scope (9 variants from 5 architecture families) and modest benchmark size (367 videos) compared to major benchmarks; generalization to future models and diverse video domains unclear

Limited mechanistic understanding of why sycophancy occurs; the paper effectively measures the phenomenon but provides insufficient analysis of underlying causes and model representations that encode sycophancy

Practical applicability concerns: key-frame selection requires knowing query-relevant frames a priori; representation steering is compute-intensive and model-specific; robustness to natural prompt variations unexplored
CRS metric analysis hampered by small sample sizes due to high first-round model accuracy, potentially limiting statistical power and introducing bias in reliability assessment
Sycophancy-inducing prompts follow somewhat stylized patterns; robustness to diverse user phrasing and subtle prompt variations not thoroughly investigated
Trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and performance on normal (non-adversarial) questions not well characterized; potential performance degradation on clean data not discussed

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: sycophancy in Video-LLMs, extending prior LLM work to the multimodal video domain with novel challenges
Well-designed benchmark with principled curation (MSS/CRS filtering), comprehensive sycophancy taxonomy (7 types across 4 linguistic categories), and robust validation (87.8% model overlap)
Thorough empirical evaluation across 9 model variants spanning diverse architectures with multi-dimensional analysis (model scale, question complexity, bias intensity) and actionable findings
Comprehensive experimental coverage including detailed ablation studies, abstention analysis, recent model evaluation (Gemini-2.5-Flash), and mechanisms analysis (attention patterns)
Two practical, training-free mitigation strategies with complementary strengths: key-frame selection (input-level, 22% MSS reduction) and representation steering (internal, 46% reduction)
Strong experimental design with proper baseline comparisons, general performance preservation analysis, and clear reproduction details using public datasets
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: sycophancy typology adapted from Sharma et al. (2024), key-frame selection is straightforward filtering, representation steering builds on Turner et al. (2023) and Zou et al. (2023)

Mitigation strategies have significant practical limitations: key-frame selection fails on LLaVA-OneVision with no deep investigation (Appendix F.5); representation steering requires white-box access, model-specific calibration, and per-model hyperparameter tuning
Benchmark scope limitations: restricted to short trimmed videos (acknowledged), only 5 topic categories, 141-video annotated subset is small, multiple-choice format may not reflect real deployments

Lack of annotation quality metrics: no inter-annotator agreement reported for question-type assignments, no gold-standard validation, potential bias from two-stage curation toward pathological edge cases rather than natural sycophancy

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: limited attention analysis (only InternVL-2.5), unclear why key-frame selection fails on some architectures, root causes of differential vulnerability not deeply explored
Missing comparative baselines: no comparison with other trustworthiness interventions beyond majority vote and contradiction checking, no analysis of mitigation strategy interactions
